title: Word order and connectives

objectives.can: Explain what καί, δέ, γάρ, οὖν, ἀλλά and μέν … δέ signal, and notice a word moved forward for emphasis.

explanation.summary: Small words join the sentences of a Greek text and tell the reader how each one relates to the last: καί adds, δέ moves on or contrasts, γάρ explains, οὖν draws a conclusion, ἀλλά corrects. Word order, which the endings leave free, is then used to put the important word in front. Both are tendencies that grammarians describe, not strict rules.

sections.heading: The common connectives
body: A connective is a word that ties a clause or sentence to what went before. Greek uses a small set of them all the time, and a translator who ignores them loses the thread of an argument or a story. The table lists the ones met here, with what each usually does and a verse to look at.

The senses are not exact equivalents of English words. καί and δέ are both often 'and' in English, but they are not the same: καί simply adds, while δέ usually marks a new step or a mild contrast. Read the verse before deciding.

Example

sections.heading: Words that never come first
body: Several of these words are postpositive: they cannot stand first in their clause. δέ, γάρ, οὖν, μέν and τε all take the second place, after the first word or the first phrase. In Matthew 2:3 the sentence begins ἀκούσας δὲ ὁ βασιλεύς: the participle comes first and δέ follows it. In Ephesians 2:8, τῇ γὰρ χάριτι, the γάρ is in second place even though that puts it between an article and its noun.

A count of the New Testament in this library agrees with the grammars: of more than four thousand occurrences of δέ, γάρ, οὖν and μέν, not one is the first word of a verse. καί and ἀλλά, by contrast, can open a sentence. The consequence for reading is that the first word of a sentence is usually not a postpositive: look past the first word for the connective.

sections.heading: μέν … δέ and οὖν
body: μέν prepares for a δέ later on. In Acts 22:9, τὸ μὲν φῶς ἐθεάσαντο τὴν δὲ φωνὴν οὐκ ἤκουσαν, the two halves are set side by side: the light was seen, the voice was not heard. English can use 'on the one hand … on the other', or simply 'while … ' or 'but', and often leaves μέν untranslated. μέν sometimes has no matching δέ, and then it only signals that something follows.

οὖν has two common jobs. It can draw a conclusion, as in Matthew 28:19 where πορευθέντες οὖν follows the statement of authority in verse 18. In narrative, particularly in John, it often just resumes the story or moves it forward. The combination μὲν οὖν, as in John 20:30, often marks the end of one stretch of text before a new turn, which comes with ταῦτα δὲ in the next verse.

sections.heading: No connective at all
body: A sentence with no connective is asyndeton. It is common in John. John 1:2 and 1:4 give the reader no particle at their beginning, and John 11:35 is the extreme case: ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς. It is a very short statement with no connective. Readers have often felt that this gives a sentence weight or abruptness, but that is a literary impression and nothing in the grammar proves it.
Asyndeton also occurs in lists and in commands. The point for reading is only to notice it and to ask how the sentence relates to the last one, since the Greek will not tell you.

sections.heading: Putting a word first
body: Greek endings show the roles of words, so the writer can choose the order for other reasons. Grammarians describe a few tendencies. A word placed early in the sentence, especially before the verb when it would not usually stand there, is often being given prominence, either as the topic that the sentence is about or as the point it makes. The reading is a matter of judgement and context.

John 1:1 is the standard example. The third clause is καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος: the noun θεός, which is the predicate, comes before the verb, and the subject ὁ λόγος comes after it. Reading it as the word order of a statement about what the Word was is a common explanation. In Ephesians 2:8, τῇ γὰρ χάριτι comes before ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι, and it is common to read this as putting the means in front. In both verses the order is a clue, and the case endings still fix who does what.

misunderstandings: Translating δέ always as 'but'. It is often only a step in the story, 'and' or 'now', and the contrast depends on the sentence.
Treating καί as always 'and'. It can also mean 'also' or 'even', and it can join things that are in tension, so that English wants 'yet'.
Looking for the connective at the head of the sentence. δέ, γάρ, οὖν and μέν come second.
Reading a rule into word order. A word at the front of a sentence is often emphasised, but it is a tendency, and many sentences are ordered by habit.

deeper.heading: Particles and discourse
body: Modern work on Greek treats these words as discourse markers: they show how the writer organises the text, not only how clauses are joined. One influential view is that δέ marks a new development in the story and that καί marks continuation. This is a description of tendency, and the lesson relies on it only as a convenient way to talk about the evidence.

deeper.heading: Semitic style and the use of καί
body: A long chain of καί, as in John 1:1 and 1:10, is often said to reflect Hebrew and Aramaic storytelling, in which clauses are strung together with a single conjunction. Others point out that Greek of the period could do the same in plain narrative. Both views can be held; a reader needs only to notice that καί links without specifying how.

examples.analysis: δέ stands in second place, after the participle ἀκούσας: a postpositive. It marks a new step in the story after the visit of the magi, and does not mean much more than 'and' or 'now'. Later in the verse καί adds a further subject: Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.

examples.analysis: The verse is a chain of three clauses joined by καί, with no other connective. In the third, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, the predicate θεός stands before the verb and the subject after it. The usual explanation is that this puts the predicate in front for prominence. The nominative endings, not the order, tell you that ὁ λόγος is the subject.

examples.analysis: γάρ is in second place, between the article τῇ and its noun χάριτί, and it signals that the verse gives the reason for what was said before. χάριτί, the dative of means, is placed ahead of the verb ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι, which is the sort of forward position that grammarians often read as emphasis on the means.

examples.analysis: διότι opens a reason clause. The two negated verbs ἐδόξασαν and ηὐχαρίστησαν are followed by ἀλλά, which turns to what happened instead: ἐματαιώθησαν. This is the usual pattern of ἀλλά, a correction after a negative. The next καί adds a second consequence.

practice.prompt: ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ Πέτρος εἶπεν τῷ Ἰησοῦ. Where does δέ stand, and what does it show?

options: First in the clause, to mark a command
Second, after the participle; it marks a new step in the story
Last in the clause, to mark a question
Second, to show that Peter is the object
practice.explain: δέ is a postpositive and takes second place. Here it moves the narrative on to Peter's reply, and 'and' or 'now' is the natural sense. It does not mark a command or a question.

practice.prompt: οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος τὸ φῶς, ἀλλ’ ἵνα μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τοῦ φωτός. What does ἀλλ’ (word 5) do?

options: It corrects the negative: 'he was not the light, but (was sent) to bear witness'
It gives a reason for the first clause
It adds a further item, as καί does
It marks a question
practice.explain: ἀλλά is the strong contrast, and after a negative statement it says what is true instead. The ἵνα clause gives the positive point. A reason would be given by γάρ.

practice.prompt: οὔπω γὰρ ἦν βεβλημένος εἰς τὴν φυλακὴν ὁ Ἰωάννης. What does γάρ (word 1) show about this sentence?

options: It gives an explanation of what has been said: the verse says why John could still be baptising
It draws a conclusion from the previous verse
It contrasts this sentence with the previous one
It begins a new, unrelated story
practice.explain: The verse before says that John was baptising in Aenon. γάρ introduces an explanation that fits the background: he was not yet in prison. A conclusion would be given by οὖν.

practice.prompt: ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν. What is δέ (word 1) doing?

options: Giving a reason, as γάρ does
Marking a strong correction, as ἀλλά does
Marking the first word of the verse
Marking a mild contrast with verse 11, where they did not receive him: 'but as many as received him'
practice.explain: Verse 11 says that his own did not receive him, and δέ turns to those who did. It is second in the clause, after ὅσοι. A strong correction would be ἀλλά, and a reason γάρ.

options: δέ must always be translated 'but'
δέ is a postpositive in second place, after the participle
δέ is a preposition governing ἀκούσας
δέ is first in the sentence and ἀκούσας comes after it
check.explain: δέ cannot stand first in its clause; it takes the second place. It is a connective and not a preposition. Its sense is only 'and' or 'now' here, not 'but'.

check.prompt: καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. Which feature of the word order do grammarians point to?

options: The order is random and has no effect
The predicate θεός stands before the verb, which is often read as giving it prominence
The verb ἦν is first, which makes the sentence a question
The subject ὁ λόγος is first, which makes it the topic
check.explain: θεός comes first in the clause, and ὁ λόγος, with the article, follows the verb. Many grammarians read the fronting as a way of giving the predicate prominence. Word order is a clue and not a proof; the cases show which word is the subject.

options: It joins two nouns, and it stands before ἐστε
It draws a conclusion, and it stands first in the sentence
It marks a contrast, and it stands last
It gives a reason or explanation, and it stands in second place, after τῇ
check.explain: γάρ is the connective for explanation ('for'), and as a postpositive it takes second place, even between an article and its noun. οὖν would draw a conclusion; ἀλλά would mark a contrast.

check.prompt: τὸ μὲν φῶς ἐθεάσαντο τὴν δὲ φωνὴν οὐκ ἤκουσαν. What do μέν and δέ do together?

options: They make the sentence a question
They set two things side by side: the light was seen, and the voice was not heard
They mark the first and second verses of a quotation
They both mean 'because'
check.explain: μέν prepares for δέ, and the pair balances two clauses. Each particle takes second place after its first phrase. They do not give a reason, and they do not turn a statement into a question.

check.prompt: οὐχ ὡς θεὸν ἐδόξασαν ἢ ηὐχαρίστησαν, ἀλλὰ ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς αὐτῶν. What does ἀλλά (word 10) signal?

options: A strong contrast: after what they did not do, what happened to them instead
A reason for the earlier verbs
A simple addition, as with καί
A question
check.explain: ἀλλά after a negative marks what is the case instead. The verbs before it are negated by οὐχ; ἐματαιώθησαν says what happened in their place.

check.prompt: Ἐδόθη μοι πᾶσα ἐξουσία … πορευθέντες οὖν μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη. What does οὖν signal?

options: A reason for the previous verse
A conclusion drawn from the previous verse: 'therefore'
That the sentence is a question
A contrast with the previous verse
check.explain: Verse 18 states the authority that has been given, and οὖν links the command to it: 'go, therefore'. It is a postpositive, second after the participle. A contrast would be ἀλλά or δέ, and a reason would be γάρ.

check.prompt: ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς. This short verse begins with no connective at all. What is this called, and what can a reader say about it with confidence?

options: Asyndeton: the sentence stands without a connective, and the reader has to ask how it relates to the last
A genitive absolute
A postpositive: it is waiting for δέ
Fronting: the verb has been moved to the end
check.explain: A sentence with no connective is asyndeton. Readers often feel that it adds weight, but that is an impression; the grammar only tells us that no link is marked. The verb ἐδάκρυσεν is first, and the subject follows.

check.prompt: Πολλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἄλλα σημεῖα ἐποίησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς … ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται ἵνα πιστεύητε. What does δέ in the second sentence do?

options: It draws a conclusion: 'so these were written'
It moves the text on and turns from the many unwritten signs to these written ones: 'but these have been written'
It gives a reason: 'for these were written'
It repeats the μέν of the first sentence
check.explain: The first sentence says that many other signs are not written in this book. μὲν οὖν there, and δέ here, mark the turn: the signs that have been recorded are written for a purpose. ταῦτα stands first as the topic.

check.prompt: Ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἦν, καὶ ὁ κόσμος δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτὸν οὐκ ἔγνω. What is the best way to understand the second καί (word 10)?

options: καί only adds; the sense of contrast ('and yet') comes from the content of the clause
καί always means 'but'
καί marks a question
καί is a postpositive, and cannot start a clause
check.explain: καί joins without saying how the clauses relate. English may want 'and yet' because the world's failure to know him follows from his making it, but that contrast is in the sense. καί can begin a clause, unlike δέ and γάρ.

reading.why: The prologue of John has καί chains (verse 1, verse 10), asyndeton (verses 2 and 4), ἀλλά after a negative (verse 8), δέ turning to a new group (verse 12) and a fronted predicate in verse 1, all in twelve verses.
